add-project: In lpm, a project is just a folder of code.
Open one from your Mac or clone one from Git,
and Claude Code works right inside it.
Open a folder is for code already on your Mac,
and Clone a repository for
code that lives in Git.
The others are for another computer or a server.
Start with code on your Mac:
click Open a folder, and the Mac's folder picker opens.
Select the folder your code is in,
here client-portal, and click Open.
lpm read the folder's package.json and found its dev server,
ready to run with Start. And client-portal is in your sidebar now,
named after its folder, with your files right where they were.
Now for code that lives in Git. Once you have a project,
new ones come in through the plus next to Projects.
Up top, Local folder and Clone repository are the same two ways in,
so choose Clone repository.
Paste the repository's URL;
on GitHub, it's under the Code button.
HTTPS or SSH both work, private repos included, with your usual Git login.
lpm names the project after the repository,
and clones it into a new folder inside the destination you choose,
here my Projects folder.
Then, click Clone repository.
A few seconds later, spoon-knife is cloned,
listed in your sidebar, and open.
Each project opens on this box,
where you start a terminal,
Claude Code, or Codex.
Pick Claude, ask what this project is,
and click Start Claude.
Claude Code runs right inside spoon-knife's folder,
so it answers from the files it finds there.
That's both ways in: Open a folder for code on your Mac,
Clone a repository for code in Git,
and for every project after your first, the plus next to Projects.
start-project: Click Start, and your whole dev stack runs in lpm,
side by side.
Click a port, and your app opens right there. No commands, no config.
client-portal runs a single dev server.
Open it, and the Start button is right up in the header.
lpm found its dev script in package.json
when you added the folder,
so there's nothing to set up: just click Start.
It runs right here, in a tab of its own,
and the bar on top shows the command lpm ran for you: npm run dev.
Its port shows right on the tab,
and in the sidebar, the project's dot is green: green means running.
To stop it, click the same button,
now a red Stop.
The server shuts down, and its dot is an empty ring again.
Now a bigger project, one that runs several services at once.
Open storefront, then the menu next to Start.
lpm found three services in its Procfile:
an API, the web app and a background worker.
It's still one button.
Click Start, and all three come up together,
each in its own tab, and the API and the web app show their ports.
Click All to watch the whole stack side by side.
When you're done, Stop takes all three down at once.
Only need the web app?
Open the menu, then click web:
it's the only one that starts,
and the only one with a green dot.
Then click the port on its tab,
and your app opens in a browser tab, right here in lpm.
One service or several: Start runs them,
Stop ends them, and there's nothing to configure.
edit-services: Your project runs a web server and an API?
Tell lpm about both, and one click starts them together.
A service is a command lpm keeps running for your project,
like a dev server.
The menu next to Start lists them.
When you added storefront,
lpm found its dev command and made it a service called web.
Two things are missing: its port, and storefront's API.
Hover web, and a pencil appears on the right. Click it to edit the service.
The form shows what lpm found:
the name, web, and the command,
npm run dev, just what you'd type in a terminal.
Under Advanced, type the port it serves on.
The gray 3000 is only an example;
storefront uses 5173.
Now lpm checks the port is free whenever you press Start.
Leave it on Ask: if something's using it,
lpm shows you what and offers to stop it.
Save changes, and back in the menu, web now shows its port.
Next, the API that lpm missed.
At the bottom of the menu, click Add service.
Name it api, and give it the command you'd run for it,
npm run api.
The preview on the right already
shows the menu with api in it.
Open Advanced again, give it port 4000, then click Add service.
Click Start, and both services run,
each in its own tab with its port.
Click All to see them side by side.
To change one while it runs,
the pencil on its bar opens this same form,
and Restart applies the change.
Click 5173 on web's bar, and the shop opens right here in lpm,
its products served by the api.
Edit what lpm found, add what it missed,
and one Start runs your whole project.
add-action: Any command you keep typing can be a one-click button.
Its output pops up right under it,
or it runs quietly in the background.
An action is a button that runs a command for you.
Claude and Codex up here are actions too,
and the plus Action button adds your own.
Click it, and a form opens.
Up top, lpm suggests commands it found,
like your package.json scripts.
Seeding the database isn't one of them, so we'll write it below.
First, the name the button will show: Seed data.
Then the command, node seed.js,
exactly as you'd type it in a terminal.
How it looks can stay as it is: a button in the header.
The preview on the right spells out what a click will do.
Under How it runs, the default opens a new terminal:
right for a server, or anything that keeps running.
Open the menu for the others:
show the output, for a quick result;
type it into the terminal you're using; or run it in the background.
Seeding is quick, and you'll want to see what it did,
so choose Run and show the output, and click Create action.
There's your button, next to Claude and Codex.
Click Seed data, and the output pops up in a card, right under it.
It seeded three customers and
twelve invoices, and the green check means it worked.
Leave it, and the card closes by itself,
but a check stays on the button: the last run passed.
Now the quick way. Click Action again, and from the suggestions,
pick Build: one click fills in the name, the command and an icon.
lpm even picked how it runs:
a build needs no watching,
so it goes in the background.
Click Create action, and Build joins the header.
Click Build, and it runs quietly while you work.
This notice in the corner turns to a check when it's done.
To change an action later, right-click it.
Edit action reopens the same form,
and Delete action removes it.
Or choose Move, then To footer,
and Build moves down to the footer bar.
A name and a command,
and anything you'd type in a terminal becomes a button in your project.
switch-profiles: Four services running when you only need two?
Save those two as a profile in lpm,
and switch with one click.
storefront has four services.
Click Start, and they all come up:
an API, the web app, a background worker, and Storybook.
Click All to see the four of them side by side.
Most days, though, you only work on the API and the web app.
The worker and Storybook just sit there, using memory.
Open the menu next to Stop.
Under Profiles, storefront already has one, called full.
A profile is a saved set of services that start together:
full runs all four, and its green dot means it's running.
Let's make a smaller one: click Add profile.
Name it everyday, then tick the two services it runs: API and web.
The preview on the right shows the menu you'll get,
with everyday just above full.
Click Add profile to save it.
Nothing restarts yet: storefront still runs all four.
Now switch to it: open the menu and click everyday.
lpm restarts storefront with just those two.
Just API and web now.
Open the menu: the green dot has moved to everyday,
and only those two services have one.
Need the whole stack again?
Click full, and all four come back.
Open the menu again: the green dot is back on full.
To change a profile later,
hover it, and its pencil opens the same form.
Make a profile for each way you work,
and switch between them with one click.
parallel-agents: Run Claude Code and Codex at the same time,
each in its own copy of your project,
so they never touch each other's files.
Here's storefront.
Claude and Codex in this one folder would edit the same files at once,
so give each agent its own copy.
Open storefront's menu in the sidebar,
choose Duplicate, and press plus for as many copies as you need, two here.
Each copy's folder gets a random tag.
Type over it to name the copy for its job:
health for the first, version for the second.
The menu beside each copy sets what runs in it.
Open the first, choose Action,
and it picks Claude, a button from your header.
Its task: add a health endpoint.
Open the second copy's menu,
choose Action, and switch it to Codex,
with a task of its own: add a version endpoint.
Each copy now shows its agent,
Claude on the first and Codex on the second,
so click Create 2 copies.
They land right under storefront,
each a full folder of its own,
and Claude is already on the first one's task.
To watch both at once, open the version copy's menu,
and choose Open side by side.
Claude on the left, Codex on the right,
each on its own task, at the same time.
In the sidebar, a check means that copy's agent is done,
and the time shows how long it took.
Commit the work you keep with each copy's Commit button,
and when you're done with a copy, open its menu and delete it.
Two, three or ten copies work the same way, with one agent in each.
multiple-accounts: Two Claude Code subscriptions on one Mac:
each project runs on its own account, and you never log out.
Claude Code keeps one login per Mac,
so a second subscription means logging out and back in.
Down in the sidebar, the Claude line is your main login,
and it has used 96% of its week.
To add a second one, open More,
then Settings, and go to Accounts & usage.
Your main login is already on the list.
Click Add, pick a name like Work,
and confirm with Add and sign in.
Claude Code's own sign-in opens,
just for this account. Finish it in your browser,
and once you're in, the bar turns green, so click Done.
Work keeps a login of its own,
so your main login stays signed in.
And each account has its own limits.
Now go back to Projects and choose who uses Work:
click the three dots next to storefront, then Claude account.
Main login has used 96% of its week,
and Work is fresh, so pick Work.
New Claude sessions in storefront now run on Work.
Click Claude in the header,
ask what this project does, and send it.
Claude answers from Work.
In the sidebar, Work gets its own meter,
and it's tagged in use: that's storefront's account.
Now click client-portal.
It's still on your main login,
so the tag moves to Claude. Open Claude here too.
Two projects on two subscriptions,
side by side, and you never logged out.
But your main login has almost no week left.
To move client-portal over,
right-click Work's line in the sidebar,
and choose Switch to Work.
The tag moves to Work.
The session that's already open keeps its login,
and every new one starts on Work.
When your main login resets,
switch back the same way:
each project stays on the account you pick.
accounts-switching: One Claude account almost out for the week?
lpm moves your new sessions to the next one on its own, and tells you why.
Down in the sidebar, the Claude line is your main login,
at 88% of its week, and it's tagged in use:
storefront's new sessions run on it.
Work, above it, is a second account, barely used.
Instead of switching by hand when one runs low,
let lpm do it.
Open More, then Settings, and go to Accounts & usage.
Further down, turn on Switch accounts automatically.
First, lpm asks you to confirm that each account is yours alone,
and the note says why: Anthropic hasn't said whether switching is allowed.
Tick Only mine, and click Turn on.
Under Turn order, only your main login takes turns so far.
Turn Work on, confirm it's yours too, and click Add.
New sessions start on the first account in the list that's under 90%
of its 5-hour and weekly limits.
Your main login is first, at 88%, so it still gets them.
Before switching, lpm asks you first,
with a note in the sidebar.
To let it move on by itself, pick Switch on its own.
Back in Projects, Work is tagged pool:
it's next in line.
Click Claude in the header, ask what this project does, and send it.
Say that reply takes your main login past 90% of its week.
lpm moves new sessions to Work on its own, and tells you why.
The in use tag moves to Work.
The session that's already open keeps going on your main login.
Open Claude again, and this new session starts on Work.
When your main login's week resets,
it's back under 90%, and new sessions return to it, first in the list.
And an account that hits a limit outright is skipped until it resets.
codex-statusline: See how much context and Codex usage you have left,
right under the prompt.
One pick in lpm sets it up.
Open a project, and click Codex in the header.
The line under its prompt is Codex's status line.
Out of the box, it shows just the model and the folder.
To change it, at the bottom of the sidebar,
click More, then Settings, and open Agents.
Scroll down to Codex status line,
below the Claude Code one, and click Customize.
At the top is a preview of the line.
Below it are ready-made layouts, so pick Usage.
Now it shows the model and the context left,
which is how much more this conversation can hold.
Next is what's left of your five-hour and weekly usage limits.
These are samples; Codex shows your own.
Below, you can drag to reorder,
remove, or add items.
Primary limit is the five-hour one,
and Secondary the weekly one.
Fast mode tells you whether Codex's
Fast mode is on.
If you don't use it, remove it.
There's no Save button: it's already saved,
and new Codex sessions pick it up.
Now head back to your project:
click the back arrow, then Projects.
The Codex you already had open keeps its old line,
so click Codex for a fresh one.
And there it is, right under the prompt:
the context left, and what's left of your five-hour and weekly limits.
Now ask Codex something,
like what this project does, and send it.
After one answer, there's already less context left.
Now one glance tells you how much room you have before you run out.
claude-statusline: See how much context and Claude Code usage you have left,
right under the prompt.
One pick in lpm sets it up.
Open the storefront project and click Claude in the header.
Ask it what this project does, and send it.
Right here, between Claude's prompt and the box you type in,
Claude Code can show a status line.
By default it's off, so there's nothing about context or usage.
To turn it on, open More at the bottom of the sidebar,
then Settings, and go to Agents.
Claude Code status line says nothing shows under the prompt yet,
so click Customize.
Up top is a live preview, empty for now.
Below it are layouts to start from.
Pick Clean, which shows context, limits and cost.
The preview shows sample
numbers. Context left, here 72 percent,
is how much room this chat still has.
Your 5-hour and weekly limits count what you've used:
34 and 62 percent.
Each meter turns yellow at 50 percent, and red at 80.
Run low on context, and Claude compacts
the chat into a summary.
Use up a limit, and Claude has to wait for the reset.
Every item can be dragged, recolored or removed.
The cost is only an estimate, so take it out.
It's gone from the preview, and Live means Claude Code already has it.
There's no save button.
Go back to Settings, then to Projects.
The Claude session that was already running picks
up the new line, with no restart.
Same spot as before, now with this chat's context left,
and how much of your 5-hour and weekly limits you've used.
Set it once, and every Claude Code session shows how much room you have left,
right where you type.
review-code-changes: Claude just edited your code.
Read every change in lpm,
undo what you don't want, and commit the rest.
Here's storefront, a small coffee shop. Click Claude in the header,
ask it for a free shipping note on the page and in the README, and send it.
Claude edits the files right in your project folder,
and the sidebar shows it working.
It commits nothing, so every change waits for you.
When it's done, click the three dots above the terminal,
and choose Review changes.
Next time, Command Shift R opens it straight away.
Every change is in one view, file by file.
On each changed line, red is how it was, and green is what Claude wrote.
On the right are the files that changed,
each marked M, for modified,
and the number on Changes counts them.
Click a file to see just that one:
its diff, or switch to File to read the whole file.
Don't want the README change?
Hover it, and click the undo arrow.
Confirm with Discard, and the file is back the way it was.
The rest looks good, so click Commit in the footer, type a message, and commit it.
The list is empty: the change is committed, and there's nothing left to review.
So whatever an agent changes,
you can read it, undo what you don't want,
and commit the rest, without leaving lpm.
action-zones: Too many buttons in your lpm header?
Stack them in a zone, flip between layers,
or fold the whole zone into one button.
Here's storefront.
Next to Claude and Codex sit five more buttons,
for builds, deploys, formatting, linting and tests.
The header has run out of room,
so they've wrapped onto a second line.
A zone fixes that:
a framed spot that stacks buttons up to three rows tall. Right-click Test,
open Move, and choose New zone with Test.
A frame takes Test's place, with Test inside.
To set it up, right-click Test again,
choose its zone, then Edit zone.
Name it Tasks: the name shows in menus,
not on the zone.
Make it two rows tall, and click Save.
Now Lint: right-click it, and under Move,
choose Into Tasks. Lint stacks under Test.
Format goes in the same way, and starts a second column:
a zone fills from top to bottom, then the next column.
A zone can also hold several sets of buttons, called layers.
Right-click the free corner of the frame,
and choose Edit zone again.
Click Add layer, and you get two.
Name the first Checks, and the second Release, then click Save.
Dots now sit under the zone, with the open layer's
name. Right-click Build, and under Move,
choose Into Tasks, Release.
The zone slides over to Release,
and Build lands there.
Move Deploy there the same way.
Now five buttons share one spot,
and the header fits on a single line again.
To go back to Checks, click the first dot.
On a trackpad, a sideways swipe over the zone flips layers too.
Need even more room?
Hover the zone, and click the small button in its corner:
the zone folds into one button, Tasks.
Hover Tasks, and its buttons pop up,
layers and all, ready to click.
Click the arrows beside it to unfold the zone again.
Everything else is in the zone's menu:
right-click its free corner.
New layer adds a layer, and Remove zone puts every button back in the header,
deleting nothing.
Zones keep related buttons together,
up to three rows tall, in the header or the footer,
and layers let one spot hold several sets of them.
connect-iphone: Send Claude Code a prompt from your iPhone, and it runs on your Mac,
at home or on cellular.
On the Mac, click the plus above your projects,
and choose Phone.
On the iPhone you need lpm Link, free on the App Store.
Turn on Remote control, and lpm Link can reach this Mac on your Wi-Fi,
while it's awake with lpm open.
Away from home, your phone can't reach it.
Built-in Tailscale fixes that:
one private network for your Mac and iPhone,
encrypted end to end, with no Tailscale app and no ports to open.
On the Mac, click Set up,
then Sign in with Tailscale.
Your browser opens Tailscale's
sign-in page, and a personal account is free.
Once you're in, the Mac is on your private network,
with an address of its own.
Now the iPhone.
In lpm Link, tap Set up Built-in Tailscale,
turn it on, and tap Sign in with Tailscale.
Sign in with the same account you use on the Mac.
Both now show it, so they're on one private network, and you can tap Done.
Now pair: your Mac shows up under On this Wi-Fi, so tap it.
The Mac asks to let this iPhone in.
The codes on both screens match,
so it's really your phone: click Allow.
lpm Link is connected, and
Away from home says Ready.
Tap Done, and your Mac's projects are on the phone.
Now for Claude Code.
On the Mac, open storefront, and
click Claude to start a session.
On the phone, tap storefront,
then its Claude tab.
The session is still on the Mac,
so tap Take control, and the Mac shows it's active on your iPhone.
Type a prompt, like what does this project do, and tap send.
Claude Code runs on your Mac, and the answer shows up right on your phone.
Back at the Mac, click Take control, and the session moves back.
Now say you leave home, and your phone is on cellular: open lpm Link.
It can't reach the Mac directly,
so it connects over Tailscale on its own,
and your projects and sessions are right there.
Remote control on the Mac,
Built-in Tailscale on both,
one pairing, and Claude Code goes wherever your phone does.
create-an-automation: Put an AI agent on a schedule:
it checks your code every weekday evening on its own, and you read what it found.
Open More at the bottom of the sidebar,
then Automations. Nothing is scheduled yet, so click New automation.
Name it Bug check.
AI prompt is already picked: an agent follows your written instructions.
Command runs one shell line instead,
and Action, once a project is picked, starts one of its actions.
Tell the agent what to do:
check the cart code for bugs, with a one-line fix for each.
At the right of the box,
pick who runs it: Claude Code with Sonnet, at Low effort, quick and cheap.
Standalone runs it in your home folder.
Open it and pick storefront.
A fresh copy or a Git worktree would leave your real folder untouched;
keep The project itself.
Nobody is there to approve its steps,
so change Full access to Read only:
it can look, but not change anything.
The same row picks which runs to report and where the results go,
and Only run when there's work can skip a quiet day.
Now, when it runs.
Choose Weekly, add Tuesday to Friday,
and set the time to six in the evening.
The footer sums it up: when the first run is,
and how it repeats. Click Create automation.
Bug check is in the list, with its project,
its schedule and its next run.
No need to wait for the evening:
open it, and click Run now.
The run starts right away,
and you can follow what the agent is doing.
It's done, and here's what it found:
the cart adds the tax twice, with a one-line fix.
Open the run to read all of it,
and reply there to ask a follow-up.
That's an automation: what it does,
where it runs, what it may change,
and when, all in one place.
run-any-ai-coding-agent: whatever you use: add it to lpm as a button and run them side by side.
Here's storefront: Claude and Codex sit in its header, one click each.
To add another, like Cursor's command line agent, click plus Action.
Name it Cursor, and type the command you'd run in a terminal: agent.
It runs in a new terminal,
as an agent should, so click Create action,
and Cursor joins Claude and Codex in the header.
Click Cursor: the real Cursor agent starts in its own tab, signed in as you.
and the two sit side by side.
Ask both the same question in their prompt boxes: what does this project do?
While they work, both show up under storefront in the sidebar,
Cursor too, each with a clock.
Both answer from the same folder,
and each row gets a check when it's done.
Gemini CLI, OpenCode, or any other agent works the same way:
a name, a command, and it's one click away.
auto-pull-complete-guide: Your teammates push, and lpm pulls their commits in for you,
waits whenever your own work is in the way,
and undoes any pull in one click.
Here are three projects your team works on.
The blue arrow next to storefront means origin has three new commits you don't have
yet. lpm checks for them in the background, every ten minutes.
Rest the pointer on it,
and a card says what's new and offers to pull for you from now on.
Choose Turn on for all projects.
storefront pulls right away,
and a note says three commits came in.
Now a teammate pushes one more commit.
There's nothing to click:
on lpm's next check, storefront pulls it in by itself, with a note of its own.
Any pull can be undone, from its note,
or later from the project's
menu: right-click storefront,
open Git, and choose Undo auto pull.
storefront is back where it was, one commit behind,
and auto pull leaves that commit alone until something newer arrives.
Auto pull never pulls over your own work.
client-portal has changes I haven't committed,
so its arrow is gray.
Rest on it, and the card says it's waiting for them.
docs has a commit of mine that isn't pushed yet,
so a pull would mix the two histories.
Auto pull leaves that to you: Sync, when you're ready.
It also waits while an agent is working in a project.
To keep a project still,
like docs, right-click it, open Git,
and under Auto pull, choose Off.
Everything else is in Settings,
and the card on any arrow links straight to it.
Check for new commits finds them,
and Auto pull is Off, Chosen, for just the projects you turn on,
or All. Below it, lpm lists the projects that differ, like docs.
Turn it on once, and your projects keep up with your team by themselves,
without ever pulling over your own work.
dynamic-action-labels: Your lpm buttons can show live info:
your last release and how long ago it was,
or anything a command prints,
and they stay current by themselves.
Here's storefront. Its Release button tags a new version,
but it doesn't say what the last one was.
Right-click it, and choose Edit action.
At the end of the name, add the newest tag and its age,
each in double braces: git dot tag,
and git dot tag age.
The action also asks which kind of release.
Open the question, and its choices use variables too:
the next patch, minor and major version.
Click Save changes.
Now the button reads Release 1.4.2,
3 days ago: lpm read both from Git.
Click it, and each choice shows the version it will make.
Keep Patch, and click Run.
The release runs in the background,
and a note in the corner says when it's done.
Seconds later, the button reads 1.4.3,
just now. Nobody edited the label: the new tag did.
A label can also show what a command prints.
Click plus Action, and in the name,
write To-dos, then the command inside a dollar sign and parentheses,
the way your shell does.
This one counts the to-do comments in src.
As the command, list them,
and under How it runs, choose Run and show the output.
Click Create action, and the new button runs its command right away.
It reads To-dos, 6.
Click it, and the output lists every one of them.
Git variables follow Git on their own.
Commands run again every minute,
and right after any background action in the project, like a release.
Double braces for what Git knows,
a dollar sign for anything else,
and your buttons stay current by themselves.
share-terminal-in-browser: Share your Claude Code tab with a link:
your teammate watches it live in their browser,
and types in it when you let them.
On the left is your Mac:
click Claude to start Claude Code in storefront.
On the right, your teammate has just a browser, no lpm.
Click Share, at the top right of the tab.
lpm makes a link and copies it for you,
so send it to your teammate in a chat or an email.
Your teammate opens the link.
With lpm installed, Open lpm takes them straight in;
without it, they click Join in browser.
They type their name, and click Ask to join.
lpm asks you first.
Both screens show the same four emoji,
so you can check it's really them, then click Let in.
Your teammate now sees your tab live, but can't type in it.
Ask Claude how checkout totals are calculated, and send it.
The answer shows up in their browser at the same moment,
encrypted all the way, so lpm's
relay in between can't read it.
To help out, they click Ask to type,
and on your Mac you click Let Sam type.
Now they send Claude a follow-up, right in your session.
The keys under their box answer Claude's questions, Control C included.
Claude answers in both places, and you see every word they typed.
Click Share again to see who's in:
Can type takes typing back from one person,
and Stop sharing ends it for everyone.
Their browser shows right away that you stopped sharing.
Share a tab, send the link,
let each person in yourself,
and choose who can type.
All your teammate needs is a browser.
claude-code-codex-remote-server: Your agents don't have to run on your Mac.
Connect a server once, and Claude Code and Codex work there,
right from the sidebar in lpm.
Click the plus above your projects, and choose Server.

and come back to finished work.
Agents in lpm run on this Mac,
so closing the lid stops them.

keeps them going while you're away.
On your laptop, click the plus and choose Another computer.

automations-that-ask-you-first: Your automation stops before it decides:
patch, minor or major?

minor or major release,

in every AI prompt automation,
lpm tells the agent how to ask,

sync-ignored-files: Git never copies your .env

Your storefront project is on this Mac and on your Mac mini,
cloned from the same repository.

so the Mac mini is missing your keys and local settings.
Right-click storefront and choose Sync Ignored Files.
At the top are the two computers it keeps the same:
this Mac, and the Mac mini.
Below is everything git ignores,
on either one, and where each file is.
Your local settings and certificates are only on this Mac.
lpm has already ticked your secrets and local config,
and left heavy folders like node_modules out.
Your .env is on both, but the Mac mini's is older.

with the values hidden: the Stripe key is new here.

Tick your ignored files once,
and every computer you work on has them.

it's five minutes by default,

six-action-button-ideas: Six buttons that show what's happening in your project:
a live number on the button, and a full chart when you point at it.
Here's storefront, a small online coffee shop,
with five of those buttons already in its header.
We'll build the sixth one together at the end.
Every button here has two parts:
the face, which shows one number and keeps it current,
and a popup, a small page that opens when you rest your pointer on it.
Bundle size shows how big your app is,
right on the button. Point at it,
and a popup shows the size of each commit and your largest packages. The dashed line
is your budget.
Now add a heavy package, and watch the button.
It jumps past the budget and turns red,
and the popup names the package that did it, so you catch it before it ships.
Orders today counts your sales as they come in.
Point at it to see the whole week and your best sellers.
Here comes a new order.
The count goes up by itself,
and the popup shows what sold. There's nothing to reload.
Tests draws one square for each run:
green passed, red failed,
so you can tell at a glance whether the last run broke something.
Point at it to see what failed,
where it failed, and which tests are slowing you down.
Server health shows how fast your dev server answers, with a line behind the number.
The popup lists each route.
Ship a slow query, and watch what happens.
The button turns red, and the route that caused it stands out.
Open issues keeps the count in front of you.
Point at it, and they're sorted by label and age,
newest first, so you can see what's waiting right from your project,
without opening a browser.
Now let's build the sixth one: commit activity. It reads your Git history,
so it works in any repo.
Open Claude Code, and describe the button you want.
Say what goes on the button, and
what goes in the popup.
Here it's a bar for each day this week, and six months of commits.
Claude writes a short script for the numbers and a small web page for the chart,
then adds the button.
And there's the sixth button,
drawn from this repo's real history.
Point at it, and the popup opens with six months of commits and the busiest folders.
That's all it takes, in Claude Code or Codex.
Each button is a short script and a small web page,
and lpm keeps them current. Pick the number you check most, and put it on a button.
